slides.text: A CLI with many commands needs a good front door. In this module you control **how commands are named and found**, which ones stay out of sight, and how the help list is organized.

Four sessions:

- **Session 1:** aliases, other names for one command
- **Session 2:** how cobra finds a command, and what it suggests when nothing fits
- **Session 3:** retiring flags, and tuning the lookup and its hints
- **Session 4:** groups in the help list
A command has one name, the first word of its `Use`. An **alias** is another name that runs the same command.
The rest of `Use`, after the name, only describes the arguments in the usage line. It never becomes part of the name or of an alias.

slides.text:
By default a word must match a name or an alias exactly. Cobra can be told to be more forgiving, and it helps when nothing matches.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
typed word:
    name or alias?  run it
    prefix matching on and
    only one name starts
    with it?        run it
    otherwise       error and hints

slides.text: Two switches loosen the lookup: one ignores the case of the word, the other accepts the start of a name. Both are variables of the `cobra` package, set once before the app runs.
When nothing fits, cobra suggests names that look alike. For old or different words that it cannot guess, a command lists its own.

exercises.title: What happens?
exercises.guide: `show` prints the command name. The user types `app sta`. What happens?
exercises.code:
cobra.EnablePrefixMatching = true
root := &cobra.Command{Use: "app"}
root.AddCommand(
    &cobra.Command{Use: "status", Run: show},
    &cobra.Command{Use: "start", Run: show},
    &cobra.Command{Use: "stop", Run: show},
)
exercises.explanation: `sta` begins both `status` and `start`, so it is ambiguous and cobra matches neither. It reports an unknown command.

exercises.explanation: An alias is another name that runs the command. `SuggestFor` only adds a word to the "Did you mean" hint, so the user still has to type `remove` or `rm`.

slides.text: A flag can be retired like a command. It keeps working, it leaves the help, and it warns the user who still types it, with a text that points to its replacement.

Cobra also lets you work with the lookup itself. A command can look a list of words up without running anything, and when a word matches nothing, the command suggests the names that look alike.

The suggestions are decided by the command that does the lookup, not by the one being suggested. The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
unknown word, in the parent:
    hints off?  none
    for each child:
        few edits from name?   suggest
        word in SuggestFor?    suggest

exercises.title: What does help list?
exercises.guide: Pick what `app --help` shows for these flags.
exercises.code:
f := root.Flags()
f.String("format", "text", "output format")
f.StringP("out", "o", "", "output file")
f.String("fmt", "", "old name of format")
f.MarkShorthandDeprecated("out", "use --out")
f.MarkDeprecated("fmt", "use --format")
exercises.explanation: A deprecated flag is left out of the help, but only its shorthand is hidden when just the shorthand is deprecated. Both still work when typed, and both warn.

slides.text:
With many subcommands, the help list is one long block. **Groups** split it into blocks with a title each.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
define a group: an id, a title
give a command the group's id

help prints:
    title of the group
        its commands

slides.text: Groups appear in the order they are added. Commands without a group go to a block of their own, after the groups.

exercises.title: What happens?
exercises.guide: The app runs `app db migrate`. What happens?
options: It runs, and migrate shows under Work: in help
It panics: db has no group with that ID
It runs, and migrate goes to the extra block
exercises.explanation: A group belongs to the command that adds it. The parent of `migrate` is `db`, which has no `work` group, so cobra panics when the app executes.
